newsitem.title: GERMANY: German tycoon faces court in corporate scandal.
newsitem.headline: German tycoon faces court in corporate scandal.

text.p: A former bricklayer who rose to become a celebrated tycoon goes on trial in Frankfurt on Monday, accused of fraud that led to the collapse of his property empire in one of Germany's biggest corporate scandals.
Juergen Schneider is charged over the collapse of his group under more than five billion marks ($3 billion) of debt.

The entrepreneur's case has already inspired a feature film and intense interest is likely to come not just from the media but also from Frankfurt's big banks, blamed by Schneider for the bankruptcy of his companies.
They deny any wrongdoing -- a view backed up by prosecutors.
Schnieder, who rode to success on the wave of a property boom following German unification, has declared that he wants to make a personal statement right at the start of the trial.
Lawyers have not yet decided whether officials of major banks, embarrassed by the apparent ease with which they doled out their billions, should be called to the witness stand.

Prosecutors allege Schneider, who was extradited from Miami in 1995 following a year-long international manhunt, fooled banks into extending credit by overstating rent income from his properties and by forging bills.

Schneider, 63, faces charges of credit fraud, serious fraud and a bankruptcy offence but prosecutors say they will only try him initially on the fraud allegations. If found guilty, he faces a maximum sentence of 15 years.
The tycoon gained fame by refurbishing historic hotels and stylish shopping malls in the post-unification property boom. But his rental income was too low to repay his debts.

The collapse of his group in 1994 sparked fears of a German real estate slump, left hundreds of small craftsmen fighting for their livelihoods and exposed the banks which had left him money to public outrage.

Germany's biggest bank, Deutsche Bank AG, which bore the brunt of criticism for loose lending and lax supervision, accepted the resignations of four executives as a result of the debacle. It maintained they had not behaved dishonourably.

Deutsche, Schneider's largest creditor with an exposure of about 1.2 billion marks, made matters worse for itself when its chief executive Hilmar Kopper dismissed as "peanuts" millions of marks Schneider owed to small tradesmen and builders.
Schneider's wife Claudia is accused of abetting a bankruptcy offence and will stand trial at a later date.
